title: Rehearse One Real Language Scenario
subtitle: Prepare the phrases and repair moves needed for one low-risk interaction.
description: Choose a real low-risk interaction in the language you are learning, prepare the minimum useful phrases plus a repair phrase, rehearse likely turns, try the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from what was difficult.

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose one low-risk interaction you are likely to face and rehearse the words needed to start, complete and repair that interaction.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Define the scenario and desired outcome, write the core request or response, add likely follow-up phrases and one repair phrase for misunderstanding, rehearse both sides aloud, use the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from the point where you hesitated or needed clarification.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which scenario did I rehearse, where did the interaction become difficult, which phrase or listening cue should I add, and what can I reuse next time?

faq.question: Which scenarios should I choose first?
faq.answer: Prefer common, low-risk interactions with a clear outcome: greeting a colleague, ordering a familiar item, asking for directions, checking a reservation, introducing a project or asking a routine service question.

faq.question: What is a repair phrase?
faq.answer: It is a phrase that keeps the interaction going when you miss something, such as asking the person to repeat, slow down, clarify a word or confirm what you understood.

faq.question: Should I rehearse medical or legal conversations this way?
faq.answer: Do not rely on informal language practice for a high-stakes interaction. Use professional interpretation, translated official material or qualified assistance when misunderstanding could materially affect health, rights, money or safety.

intro.html: A broad goal such as speak better is difficult to rehearse. A specific interaction gives practice a visible beginning and end. Prepare the language required for one real low-risk scenario, include a way to repair misunderstanding, then update the script from the part that was actually difficult.

sections.title: 1. Define the interaction
sections.html: Name the setting, the other person's role and the concrete outcome you need: place an order, ask a routine question, confirm a time, introduce a topic or obtain simple information. Keep the first scenario narrow enough to rehearse end to end.

sections.title: 2. Prepare the core and repair language
sections.html: Write the opening, main request or response, likely follow-up and a repair phrase. Prefer reusable sentence frames over a long memorized speech, and leave room to substitute names, times, objects or places.

sections.title: 3. Rehearse both sides
sections.html: Say your lines aloud and imagine more than one plausible reply. Practice the repair phrase as part of the scenario so a missed word or unexpected answer does not end the interaction.

sections.title: 4. Update from the real interaction
sections.html: After using the scenario, note where you hesitated, misunderstood or lacked a phrase. Add only the language that would have helped at that point, then reuse the revised version when the same situation returns.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported language-learning effects, fabricated classroom and pilot outcomes, rigid phrase counts and repetition schedules, anxiety claims and unsafe pharmacy examples with a bounded scenario-rehearsal workflow.
